reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Follows ingestion of pufferfish (fugu) or other tetrodotoxin-containing seafood, especially when improperly prepared
Symptoms begin within minutes to a few hours with perioral and lingual paraesthesiae, then spread to the face and extremities
Progresses to nausea, vomiting, ascending flaccid paralysis, bulbar weakness and respiratory failure in severe cases
Consciousness is usually preserved even in advanced paralysis, as the toxin has limited central effect
There is no antidote; management is supportive with airway protection and mechanical ventilation until the toxin clears
Early gastrointestinal decontamination may be considered soon after ingestion, and cardiovascular support given for hypotension and bradyarrhythmia
Severity grading based on progression of paraesthesiae, weakness and cardiorespiratory signs helps guide monitoring and disposition
reference.pathophysiology: Tetrodotoxin is a potent, heat-stable toxin concentrated in the liver, gonads, skin and viscera of pufferfish and produced by symbiotic bacteria. It binds with high affinity to voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve and skeletal muscle membranes, blocking sodium influx and preventing action potential generation and propagation. The result is a rapidly progressive sensory disturbance and flaccid paralysis, including of the respiratory muscles, with respiratory failure the main cause of death. Autonomic effects can cause hypotension and bradycardia, while relative sparing of the central nervous system leaves consciousness intact.
additionalDifferentials: Other cause of acute neuromuscular respiratory failure
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on ingestion history and characteristic progression
Continuous respiratory monitoring and serial forced vital capacity
Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases for ventilatory failure
Electrocardiography and cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmia
Electrolytes and baseline bloods to exclude alternative causes
Toxin detection in food or biological samples where laboratory capability exists
redFlags: Spreading paraesthesiae with progressive limb and bulbar weakness
Declining respiratory effort or oxygen saturation
Rapid symptom onset after ingestion (suggesting a large dose)
Preserved awareness with advancing paralysis heralding respiratory arrest
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on timely airway and ventilatory support; patients who survive the first hours with adequate ventilation generally recover fully within days, whereas untreated respiratory failure is rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Underestimating the speed of progression from paraesthesiae to respiratory failure
Assuming immobility reflects unconsciousness, when awareness is usually retained
Waiting for an antidote instead of instituting supportive ventilation
Failing to recognise the diagnosis in the absence of a clear pufferfish history
management: There is no antidote; the mainstay is meticulous airway protection with early intubation and mechanical ventilation, as respiratory-muscle paralysis is the main cause of death
Consider early gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal soon after ingestion
Treat autonomic instability with intravenous fluids and vasopressors for hypotension and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
Continuous respiratory and cardiac monitoring with serial forced vital capacity to detect deteriorating ventilation
Provide supportive intensive care until the toxin clears, with full recovery expected in survivors who are adequately ventilated
Manage in a critical care setting with early escalation for ventilatory failure
